results.name: heterogeneity_growth_with_set_size
results.description: Between-participant SD (participants = trial_index resets; each participant's rate minus their 5-person design batch mean) of the yes-rate on out-of-span non-example targets in 3-4-example sets, minus the same SD for 1-example sets; observed above null_mean means individual differences grow with set size more than the model's per-person range looseness produces (below = the model over-predicts that growth).
results.code:
# name: heterogeneity_growth_with_set_size
# description: Between-participant SD (participants = trial_index resets; each participant's rate minus their 5-person design batch mean) of the yes-rate on out-of-span non-example targets in 3-4-example sets, minus the same SD for 1-example sets; observed above null_mean means individual differences grow with set size more than the model's per-person range looseness produces (below = the model over-predicts that growth).
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.diff(ti) < 0)])
    batch = pid // 5
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    out = (t < np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) | (t > np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    def sd(mask):
        d = pd.DataFrame({"p": pid[mask], "b": batch[mask], "y": y[mask]})
        pr = d.groupby(["b", "p"])["y"].mean().reset_index()
        if len(pr) < 3:
            return 0.0
        pr["dev"] = pr["y"] - pr.groupby("b")["y"].transform("mean")
        return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(pr["dev"] ** 2)))
    return sd(out & (n >= 3)) - sd(out & (n == 1))

results.name: single_example_shared_digit
results.description: For 1-example sets, among non-example targets more than 10 away from the example, yes-rate for targets sharing any digit with the example minus targets sharing none; observed above null_mean means people generalize from one number by surface digit overlap more than the model's contains-digit/final-digit rules produce (below = less).
results.code:
# name: single_example_shared_digit
# description: For 1-example sets, among non-example targets more than 10 away from the example, yes-rate for targets sharing any digit with the example minus targets sharing none; observed above null_mean means people generalize from one number by surface digit overlap more than the model's contains-digit/final-digit rules produce (below = less).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    e = ex[:, 0]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    sel = (n == 1) & (np.abs(t - e) > 10)
    e_i = np.where(sel, e, 0).astype(int)
    def digits(v):
        D = np.zeros((len(v), 10), dtype=bool)
        r = np.arange(len(v))
        D[r, v % 10] = True
        tens = (v // 10) % 10
        D[r, tens] |= (v >= 10)
        D[r, 1] |= (v == 100)
        D[r, 0] |= (v == 100)
        return D
    share = (digits(e_i) & digits(t)).any(axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = sel & share
    b = sel & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: outside_edge_gradient
results.description: For 2+-example sets, among out-of-span targets, yes-rate when the target is 1-4 beyond the nearest span edge minus when it is 15+ beyond; observed above null_mean means generalization falls off just outside the examples' span more steeply than the model's interval posterior produces (below = shallower, i.e. people extend further).
results.code:
# name: outside_edge_gradient
# description: For 2+-example sets, among out-of-span targets, yes-rate when the target is 1-4 beyond the nearest span edge minus when it is 15+ beyond; observed above null_mean means generalization falls off just outside the examples' span more steeply than the model's interval posterior produces (below = shallower, i.e. people extend further).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    near = (n >= 2) & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 4)
    far = (n >= 2) & (dist >= 15)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[near].mean() - y[far].mean())

results.name: person_inspan_outspan_correlation
results.description: Across participants (trial_index resets; rates centred on their 5-person design batch), correlation between a person's yes-rate on in-span non-example targets and on out-of-span targets, in 2+-example sets; observed above null_mean means people carry a shared generalization-breadth/yes-bias trait the model lacks, below means a trade-off (range fill-in vs rule extension) stronger than the model's per-person range looseness produces.
results.code:
# name: person_inspan_outspan_correlation
# description: Across participants (trial_index resets; rates centred on their 5-person design batch), correlation between a person's yes-rate on in-span non-example targets and on out-of-span targets, in 2+-example sets; observed above null_mean means people carry a shared generalization-breadth/yes-bias trait the model lacks, below means a trade-off (range fill-in vs rule extension) stronger than the model's per-person range looseness produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.diff(ti) < 0)])
    batch = pid // 5
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = (n >= 2) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~isex
    out = (n >= 2) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    def rates(mask):
        d = pd.DataFrame({"p": pid[mask], "b": batch[mask], "y": y[mask]})
        pr = d.groupby("p").agg(y=("y", "mean"), b=("b", "first"))
        pr["y"] = pr["y"] - pr.groupby("b")["y"].transform("mean")
        return pr["y"]
    a = rates(ins); b = rates(out)
    j = a.index.intersection(b.index)
    if len(j) < 4:
        return 0.0
    x = a.loc[j].to_numpy(); z = b.loc[j].to_numpy()
    if x.std() == 0 or z.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, z)[0, 1])

results.name: example_target_endorsement_by_set_size
results.description: Yes-rate on targets that are one of the shown examples in 3-4-example sets minus in 1-example sets; observed below null_mean means people disown examples of larger sets (treat some as strays) more than the model's constant 10% stray rate implies (above = less).
results.code:
# name: example_target_endorsement_by_set_size
# description: Yes-rate on targets that are one of the shown examples in 3-4-example sets minus in 1-example sets; observed below null_mean means people disown examples of larger sets (treat some as strays) more than the model's constant 10% stray rate implies (above = less).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = isex & (n >= 3)
    b = isex & (n == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: congruence_beyond_parity
results.description: For 3-4-example sets whose sorted differences share a gcd g in {4,6,8,12} with examples not multiples of g (progressions like 41,47,53), yes-rate on non-example targets congruent to the examples mod g minus same-parity non-congruent targets; observed above null_mean means people extract step/progression rules (beyond parity) that the model's fixed rule set under-produces.
results.code:
# name: congruence_beyond_parity
# description: For 3-4-example sets whose sorted differences share a gcd g in {4,6,8,12} with examples not multiples of g (progressions like 41,47,53), yes-rate on non-example targets congruent to the examples mod g minus same-parity non-congruent targets; observed above null_mean means people extract step/progression rules (beyond parity) that the model's fixed rule set under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    from functools import reduce
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    info = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        a = sorted(int(x) for x in s.split(","))
        g = 0
        r = -1
        if len(a) >= 3:
            g = reduce(math.gcd, [b - a[0] for b in a[1:]])
            if g in (4, 6, 8, 12) and a[0] % g != 0:
                r = a[0] % g
            else:
                g = 0
        info[s] = (g, r, a[0] % 2)
    g = sets.map(lambda s: info[s][0]).to_numpy()
    r = sets.map(lambda s: info[s][1]).to_numpy()
    par = sets.map(lambda s: info[s][2]).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    gs = np.where(g > 0, g, 1)
    ok = (g > 0) & ~isex & (t % 2 == par)
    cong = ok & (t % gs == r)
    non = ok & (t % gs != r)
    if cong.sum() == 0 or non.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[cong].mean() - y[non].mean())

results.name: magnitude_scaled_extension
results.description: Yes-rate on targets 1-10 outside the examples' span for sets whose example mean is >= 60, minus the same for sets whose mean is <= 40; observed above null_mean means people extend further around large numbers (log/compressed number line) than the model's uniform-width intervals predict (below = the reverse).
results.code:
# name: magnitude_scaled_extension
# description: Yes-rate on targets 1-10 outside the examples' span for sets whose example mean is >= 60, minus the same for sets whose mean is <= 40; observed above null_mean means people extend further around large numbers (log/compressed number line) than the model's uniform-width intervals predict (below = the reverse).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    mu = np.nanmean(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    band = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 10)
    big = band & (mu >= 60)
    small = band & (mu <= 40)
    if big.sum() == 0 or small.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[big].mean() - y[small].mean())

results.name: rule_discrimination_four_examples
results.description: For 4-example sets whose examples all fit a small rule (multiples of m=3..12, squares, powers of 2, or a shared final digit; smallest such rule), yes-rate on out-of-span rule-member targets minus out-of-span non-member targets; observed above null_mean means people follow the rule beyond the span more sharply than the model at n=4 (below = the model over-commits to the rule).
results.code:
# name: rule_discrimination_four_examples
# description: For 4-example sets whose examples all fit a small rule (multiples of m=3..12, squares, powers of 2, or a shared final digit; smallest such rule), yes-rate on out-of-span rule-member targets minus out-of-span non-member targets; observed above null_mean means people follow the rule beyond the span more sharply than the model at n=4 (below = the model over-commits to the rule).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    rules = [set(range(m, 101, m)) for m in range(3, 13)]
    rules.append({k * k for k in range(1, 11)})
    rules.append({2 ** k for k in range(0, 7)})
    rules += [{x for x in range(1, 101) if x % 10 == d} for d in range(10)]
    memb = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        a = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        best = None
        if len(a) == 4:
            for R in rules:
                if all(x in R for x in a) and (best is None or len(R) < len(best)):
                    best = R
        memb[s] = np.array([(k in best) if best is not None else False for k in range(101)])
        memb[s] = (memb[s], best is not None)
    has = sets.map(lambda s: memb[s][1]).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    M = np.stack([memb[s][0] for s in sets.unique()])
    idx = pd.Index(sets.unique()).get_indexer(sets)
    mem = M[idx, t]
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    out = (t < np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) | (t > np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = has & out & mem
    b = has & out & ~mem
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
